PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 8

Fruits & Vegetables

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 8Subjects Fruits & vegetables

Sixteen cards about the foods your child already knows: eight fruits, eight vegetables. Meet them all, sort them into their bowls, find them, match them, line them up by color and count them together — this class follows Body Parts & My Five Senses on the preschool path.

Food words are words children use three times a day. You say the name, your child finds the real thing in the kitchen — and suddenly the flashcards and the fruit bowl are the same game.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, snack nearby — both help.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Five little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, all sixteen food cards, colors and counting, solving the food sheets together, off-screen kitchen play, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  1. 1 Teacher welcome
  2. 2 Meet the foods
  3. 3 Colors & counting
  4. 4 Solve the sheets
  5. 5 Take it off screen
  6. 6 Class complete
TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend — and hello to you, grown-up helper! Today’s class smells wonderful: sixteen foods are waiting — fruits for one bowl, vegetables for the other, and a whole rainbow to count. Wash your hands and let’s begin!”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

Begin the class ↓First stop: the whole market, sixteen cards long.
MEET THE FOODS

Sixteen foods, one happy market.

Say each food’s name as it arrives, then hunt for the real one in your kitchen later — the pair is the whole lesson. Use the arrows to wander, or simply scroll: all sixteen cards are below.

Card 1 of 16
Or simply scroll: all 16 cards are below.

Say it, then spot it

  • After every few cards, ask “where do we keep the…?” — bananas on the counter, carrots in the drawer. Food words live in places.
COLORS & COUNTING

A rainbow you can eat.

Foods come in every color. Read each row together, count the cards in it, then try the counting games below — all of them use the sixteen cards you already met.

  • Red foods

    Three red foods — count them: one, two, three!

  • Yellow foods

    Three yellow foods — count them again!

  • Orange foods

    Three orange foods — the color and the fruit share a name on one of them.

  • Green foods

    Three green foods — two of them crunch, one is sweet.

  • Purple & brown foods

    One purple bunch, two brown friends — three cards in this row.

Count together

  • Count the fruits: apple, banana, orange, strawberry, grapes, watermelon, pineapple, mango — eight fruits!
  • Count the vegetables: carrot, potato, tomato, cucumber, broccoli, corn, onion, pumpkin — eight too!
  • Count any row in the chart above — three foods in every row. Which color is your favorite?
  • Watermelon seeds and pumpkin seeds: too many to count — counting them anyway is the fun part.
SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the food sheets together.

The sixteen food cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all sixteen, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each food as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Fruit or vegetable?

    Sort the cut cards into two bowls — fruits here, vegetables there. Scientists sort the tomato with the fruits, cooks sort it with the vegetables — both are right.

  3. 03

    Count the bowls

    Count the cards in each bowl together. Then line them up by color: a red row, a green row, a yellow row.

  4. 04

    Find them in the kitchen

    Take two or three cards to the real kitchen and find their twins in the fruit bowl. Then color a favourite card with the Write & Color layer.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

OFF-SCREEN PLAY

The kitchen is the classroom.

Food words are kitchen words. Pick one of these — five minutes is plenty — and let your child lead the hunt.

The kitchen food hunt

  • Take three cards — say an apple, a carrot and a corn — and hunt the kitchen for each one. Hold the real food next to its card: same, same, same!

Two bowls, for real

  • Set out two bowls and sort the actual shopping: fruit in one, vegetables in the other. The sorting game from today, played with things you can eat afterwards.

Market twin hunt

  • Take one card to the shop or market and find its twin in the pile. One matched carrot is a whole class.

Wash it together

  • Before any tasting, wash the fruits and vegetables together at the sink. Rubbing a shiny apple dry is a food-hygiene habit that starts here — and a quiet color-and-count moment too.

One safety word for this class: wash foods before touching mouths, grown-ups do all the cutting, whole grapes and cherry tomatoes are cut small for little mouths, and everyone sits down while eating. Tasting is for real food a grown-up has checked — never anything found on the floor or offered by curiosity.

PRINT THE CARDS

Take the market to the kitchen table.

All sixteen cards print two to a page, in card order, straight from your browser — no PDF, nothing to install. Cut them out and the whole market plays on the table.

View Printable Cards ↗

Printed cards love fridges, snack cups and shopping bags. The same cards also live in the flashcards library, each with its own page.

“What a delicious class! Your child named fruits, sorted vegetables, matched twins and counted a whole rainbow of foods — that is real vocabulary, real math and real healthy-eating practice, all in one. Keep the game alive at every meal: name it, find it, count it. See you in class!”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Naming and sorting food does something quietly powerful: it makes unfamiliar foods familiar before they ever reach the plate. A child who has said “broccoli”, matched its card and held a real one is far more likely to try a bite — curiosity does the persuading, not pressure. Keep meals free of scores and negotiations: the game is naming, finding, washing and counting, and a food that is only looked at today still counts as a win.

Delicious work!

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Say the word and hold the real food — the pair is what sticks. “Carrot!” while you both touch a carrot in the drawer teaches faster than the screen alone, because the kitchen makes the word true. Let your child take every tap and every sort, even when the answer looks obvious: the finger teaches the mind.

Then flip the game: your child says a food word and YOU hunt for it. Getting one wrong on purpose — “this tomato is actually an apple, look!” — keeps the sorting game alive for weeks, and being the caller is powerful practice for a three-year-old.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was one banana and two claps, today’s class was a success.

FROM THE FRUIT BOWL

Four of this class’s words play in Look & Learn.

Banana, carrot, grapes and strawberry all appear in Look & Learn, the fifteen-card deck where every picture carries a move: peel the banana, pull the carrot from the ground, step in a puddle by the boot. A fruit word your child can name here often lands there first as a game — and the pear, lemon and tomato cards make a good second bowl.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The apple opens the fruit class because it is the fruit most children already own: it sits in their fruit bowl, their lunchbox, their stories. This lesson gives the word a home, the fruit a biography — it grows on trees — and your child a crunchy, washed-and-ready tasting job.

    What is this?

    An apple is a round fruit that grows on trees, in orchards and gardens, hanging from branches until picked. On the card it is a shiny red apple with a green leaf. In your kitchen it is heavy and cold in the hand, crunchy between the teeth, and sweet enough to request by name.

    What does it mean?

    Naming a food your child already eats turns snack time into lesson time: the word apple gets attached to the heaviest, coldest, crunchiest fruit in the bowl, and every future apple repeats it. Food words are the easiest vocabulary a kitchen teaches, because the props show up daily and get eaten on schedule.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, one real apple held in both hands — heavy, smooth, cold — and one supervised tasting: washed under the tap, cut by a grown-up into slices, then crunched loudly together. The loud crunch is not optional; it is the sound of the lesson working.

    Why this matters

    Apples are a first lesson in where food comes from: not shelves, but trees, seasons and picking. A child who says “apples grow on trees” has planted the seed of a food story that will grow into gardens, farms and why-we-wash-things — real knowledge with a snack attached.

    What it teaches

    Word-object mapping with a holdable prop, early food-science (tree to table), sensory vocabulary (heavy, smooth, cold, crunch), counting at the fruit bowl, and the confidence of requesting food by name.

    Words to learn

    appleredroundcrunchtreeseed

    Say this to your child

    ““Apple! Here is the picture apple, all shiny with its leaf. Can you find the real one? Feel it — heavy! Cold! Now we wash it, a grown-up cuts it, and... CRUNCH! Did you hear that? That is the sound of an apple saying hello.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say apple — then ask your child to find the real thing in the fruit bowl before you lift a finger.
    2. Hand the apple over: heavy, smooth, cold. Say the word while both hands are full — the grip is the vocabulary lesson.
    3. Tell the biography: apples grow on trees, hung there by the tree itself, picked when round and ready.
    4. Tasting job: your child washes the apple under the tap while you cut it into slices, then everyone crunches as loudly as possible.
    5. Count the apples left in the bowl together — the word got said, the fruit got eaten, and the numbers sneaked in behind both.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a shiny red apple with a green leaf and the word apple underneath. Ask your child where the leaf sits, what color the apple is, and whether the real apple in your bowl wears a leaf too.

    Ask your child

    “Where do apples grow — on trees or under the ground?” “Is the apple heavy or light?” “What sound does a crunch make?” “Should we wash it first — why?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might demand “apple slices, please!” at odd hours, report that the apple is cold like the fridge, or march to the tap uninvited to wash the next one — a food word that triggers its own safety routine is a food word fully learned.

    Out in the real world

    Apples repeat all week: at breakfast, in the lunchbox, at the shop where the pile sits shiny and cold. Each one is a rehearsal of the word — and by the time the bag is empty, it has been crunched into memory.

    Try it together

    Apple bowl hide-and-seek: hide three apples around the room while your child counts to ten, then send them hunting with the word — “find an apple!” Every discovery gets announced, washed and shared. The hunt is cardio; the naming is the lesson.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Where does an apple grow? What do we do before we eat it? Show me a crunch.” Tree, wash and a jaw-breaking demonstration — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child rejects the first slice, offer the crunch challenge instead: who can make the loudest sound? Pride reopens more mouths than persuasion ever will, and the second bite is usually the one that counts.

    Staying safe

    Apples get washed before every tasting, and a grown-up does all the cutting — slices, not chunks, for small mouths. Whole apples are for confident chewers at the table, never for wandering-and-munching, and a wobbly-toothed cruncher gets their slices thinner.

    This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Banana — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The banana is the fruit a three-year-old can open all by themselves, which makes it a milestone wearing a snack. This lesson teaches the word at the card, the growing — tall plants in warm countries, not trees — and hands over the peel, the proudest job in the fruit bowl.

    What is this?

    A banana is a long, curved, yellow fruit that grows in bunches on tall plants in warm countries. The card shows one yellow banana with the word underneath. Inside the peel it is soft and sweet; outside it turns from green to yellow to spotty as it ripens — spots mean sweeter.

    What does it mean?

    Peeling is problem-solving: pinch the top, pull the strip down, repeat. A child who works a banana open is doing fine-motor engineering with an edible result, and the word banana rides on every step — said at the pinch, said at the pull, said with a full mouth at the end.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the where-it-grows story — big plants, warm places, bunches — and one full peel done by their own hands while you supervise only the eating. The ripeness game is a bonus: green means wait, yellow means go, spots mean sweetest of all.

    Why this matters

    Self-service foods build independence at exactly the age it is cheapest to build: a banana needs no knife, no grown-up strength and no waiting. The word attaches to capability — “I can open it myself” — and capability is the hook that keeps vocabulary coming back.

    What it teaches

    Fine motor control in the peel, sequencing (pinch, pull, open, eat), ripeness observation, tropical-plant knowledge (big plants, not trees), and the independence that makes snack time self-managing.

    Words to learn

    bananayellowpeelsoftsweetcurve

    Say this to your child

    ““Banana! Ba-na-na — three claps for three parts. Where does it grow? On tall, tall plants, hanging in bunches in the sunshine. Now the best bit: you peel it. Pinch the top... pull the strip... open! Yellow all the way through. You opened it yourself!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say banana slowly — three parts, three claps: ba-na-na. Clap it again together.
    2. Ask where it grows and tell the story: tall green plants in warm countries, bananas hanging in whole bunches like crowds of friends.
    3. Hand over the fruit and the job: your child pinches the top and peels the strip down — help only if the pinch fails twice.
    4. Say the word at every stage: banana in the hand, banana in the peel, banana in the smile.
    5. Finish with the spots game: find the spottiest banana in the bowl and guess whether it is the sweetest — then taste the evidence.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card together: it shows a yellow banana, bent like a smile, with the word banana underneath. Ask your child which way the curve bends, what color it is, and whether the real bananas at home bend the same way.

    Ask your child

    “Do bananas grow on trees or on big plants?” “What color is a banana before it is ready?” “What do the spots mean?” “Who can peel one — you or me?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might clap out ba-na-na at random meals, inspect every banana in the shop for spots, or peel one with exaggerated ceremony for a visiting teddy — the word has landed when the routine travels to an audience.

    Out in the real world

    Bananas arrive weekly and get opened daily: breakfast, snacks, the shopping bag. Each peel is another rehearsal of the word and another rep for the fingers that do it — vocabulary and fine motor, sharing one snack.

    Try it together

    Peel-it-like-a-pro practice: two bananas, and your child opens both — pinch the top, pull the strip down, one strip at a time — while you supervise the eating. Save the peels for a teddy-bear picnic afterwards, where the word gets performed to an audience of one very polite bear.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What grows on tall plants in warm places? Clap the word. Who peels it?” The claps, the plants and a proudly opened fruit — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child calls every yellow food banana, spread the evidence: a lemon, a pepper, the banana itself — same color, different shapes. Sorting by shape after sorting by color is the next chapter, and the fruit bowl teaches it for free.

    Staying safe

    A grown-up takes over if the peel fights back, and the fruit gets a quick rinse before peeling — hands touch the outside, then the inside. Watch for over-enthusiastic bites: a banana is soft, but a full mouth still needs sitting down and slowing up.

    This lesson pairs with the Banana flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Orange — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The orange is the word-learning cheat: its name and its color are the same word, so every time your child says the fruit they are also practising the color. This lesson adds the smell — the peel’s perfume arrives before anything is even open — and the segments, which count beautifully.

    What is this?

    An orange is a round citrus fruit that grows on trees in sunny places, wearing a dimpled peel. The card shows a round orange with a green leaf. Under the peel sit segments in their own thin coats, and the smell — pressed out by little hands rolling it — starts before the first strip comes off.

    What does it mean?

    One word with two meanings doubles its airtime: orange the fruit at snack, orange the color at craft. A child who holds both meanings has met homonyms — words that wear two hats — years before the word homonym exists, and the fruit bowl demonstrated it with smell included.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the roll-and-sniff trick — rolling the fruit on the table presses oil into the peel and wakes the smell — and one shared peel-and-count: a grown-up starts the peel, small hands pull strips, and the segments get counted before they vanish.

    Why this matters

    Smell is the most underrated sense in vocabulary work: scent memories are strong and sticky, and a word that arrives with perfume attached gets a second anchor in the brain. Roll, sniff, peel, count — four senses doing the work of one word.

    What it teaches

    Olfactory vocabulary (smell, sniff, scent), fine motor in the peeling, counting the segments, two-meaning word awareness (fruit and color), and the table science of why rolling wakes a smell.

    Words to learn

    orangepeelsmellroundsegmentsjuicy

    Say this to your child

    ““Orange! The fruit with two jobs — it is a fruit AND a color. Roll it, roll it... now sniff your hands! Can you smell the sunshine? Now we peel: strip by strip. And inside — look — little boats! Let us count the boats before we eat them.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say orange — then hold up a real one and ask what else the word can mean. Let your child discover the double meaning.
    2. The smell trick: roll the orange firmly on the table, then sniff your palms together — the perfume lives in the peel, and rolling wakes it.
    3. A grown-up scores the peel; your child pulls the strips off, one by one, saying the word at every piece.
    4. Split the segments out and count them together before eating — then allow the loud, juicy munching.
    5. Close with the color round-up: what else in the kitchen is orange? The carrot card is coming, and it will match.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a round orange with a green leaf and the word orange underneath. Ask your child whether the fruit on the card is whole, where the leaf attaches, and what the real orange’s skin feels like next to the card’s smooth picture.

    Ask your child

    “Can one word mean two things?” “What color is an orange?” “Where does the smell live — the peel or the inside?” “How many segments did we count?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might roll every orange in the shop “to wake it up”, announce the smell before anyone asks, or correct you when you call the carrot an orange — “no, that is a carrot, it is ORANGE” — one word, two meanings, both in service.

    Out in the real world

    Oranges repeat all winter: the fruit bowl, the juice at breakfast, the smell on a grown-up’s hands after peeling. Every appearance rehearses both meanings — the fruit and the color — and the smell always gets top billing.

    Try it together

    The sniff station: roll two oranges on the table, sniff your palms, and vote on which smells sunnier. Then a grown-up scores the peel, your child pulls the strips off, and the segments get counted into two bowls before the loud, juicy munching begins. Smell, count, eat — the whole lesson in one snack.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What two things is an orange? Where does the smell come from? Count the boats.” The double word, the woken perfume and a counted segment — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child will not smell the peel, do not insist — sniff your own hands theatrically and wait. Curiosity about why your face is doing that usually wins inside a minute, and self-discovered smells stick harder than instructed ones.

    Staying safe

    A grown-up starts the peel with a small knife-score so small fingers have an edge to grip; the fruit itself gets rinsed before peeling, because hands travel from peel to mouth. Segments for the smallest eaters get their stringy coats removed first.

    This lesson pairs with the Orange flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Strawberry — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The strawberry is the fruit with its seeds on the outside — a fact children find hilarious and remember for years. Here the word is learned at the card, the growing story runs along the ground — low plants, sprawled in the dirt, where slugs also shop — and the seed count is done with eyes only before anyone washes or eats.

    What is this?

    A strawberry is a small, heart-shaped, bright red berry that grows on low leafy plants near the ground. The card shows a bright red strawberry with seeds and a green crown. The seeds sit ON the outside — hundreds of them — which is why the skin feels bumpy and looks speckled.

    What does it mean?

    Outside-in seeds make the strawberry a botanical celebrity: it is the exception children meet first. A child who knows that strawberries wear their seeds out loud and apples hide theirs inside has started collecting exceptions — and exception-hunting is real science, started at snack level.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the low-growing story — strawberries do not climb, they sprawl near the dirt — and one eyes-only seed hunt before tasting: how many seeds can you count? Too many! That is the answer, and it is correct every time. Then a grown-up washes and hulls, and everyone eats.

    Why this matters

    Looking closely before eating trains observation on a willing subject: the seeds are countable, visible, funny. Fine visual work disguised as a giggle builds the careful-looking habit that later finds differences in letters, numbers and faces.

    What it teaches

    Close observation with a target (seeds), exception knowledge in botany, fine motor in hulling, counting practice that happily fails (too many!), and patient waiting while the grown-up does the cutting.

    Words to learn

    strawberryredseedscrownsweetsummer

    Say this to your child

    ““Strawberry! Straw-ber-ry — what a long word for something so small. Look at it: red all over, wearing a little green crown. And here is the secret — the seeds are on the OUTSIDE! Count them with your eyes... too many! That is why it is bumpy. Now wash them, and a grown-up will do the crowns.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say strawberry in three parts — straw-ber-ry — a long word for a small berry, said three times.
    2. Tell the growing story: strawberries grow on low plants close to the ground, hiding under leaves — shoppers include slugs, which is why we wash.
    3. The seed hunt, eyes only: look at the card, then at a real strawberry — how many seeds can you count? Too many! They live OUTSIDE. Say it like news.
    4. Tasting job: your child washes the berries in the colander while a grown-up pulls the green crowns off and slices them.
    5. Eat together and rank the sweetness — was the reddest one the sweetest? Let the jury decide.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card together: it shows a bright red strawberry with seeds and a green crown, with the word strawberry underneath. Ask your child where the seeds sit — on the skin or hidden inside — and what the green crown looks like to them.

    Ask your child

    “Where do strawberries grow — up high or down low?” “Which fruit wears its seeds on the outside?” “What is the green top called?” “Why do we wash them before we eat?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might announce the outside-seeds fact to anyone who will listen, count seeds at breakfast with total sincerity, or refuse hulled berries in favor of ones “with their crowns still on” — gardeners call that last one correct.

    Out in the real world

    Strawberries are seasonal celebrities: the shop punnets in summer, the pick-your-own fields, the plants some families grow in pots. Any real meeting is a rehearsal — and the outside-seeds fact renews itself at every single one.

    Try it together

    Seed-spotting detectives: one strawberry each, examined with eyes only — how many seeds can you count before giving up? Then the washing job: your child rinses them in the colander while a grown-up pulls the crowns and slices, and the berries get ranked by redness before the first bite.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Where do strawberries grow? Where do they keep their seeds? Who takes the crowns off?” Low plants, outside-seeds and “the grown-up” — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child meets a white-streaked or pale berry, teach the honest version: strawberries wear different amounts of red depending on the sun they caught. Same fruit, same seeds, same deliciousness — the color is a weather report.

    Staying safe

    Strawberries get rinsed before anything else — they grow close to the ground, and the crowns hold grit. A grown-up pulls the crowns and slices what needs slicing; whole berries are for confident chewers, and the smallest mouths get theirs quartered.

    This lesson pairs with the Strawberry flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Grapes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Grapes are the fruit of many: one word, dozens of little balls, and a built-in sharing game — one for you, one for me. Vines are where this lesson grows from — climbing plants, heavy hanging bunches — and its kitchen half is the routine that makes grapes safe: washed first, cut small by a grown-up, eaten sitting down.

    What is this?

    A grape is a small, round, smooth fruit that grows in bunches on vines — climbing plants that farms and gardens train along wires and walls. The card shows a bunch of purple grapes. Green grapes and purple grapes are the same fruit in different dresses, and both hang in bunches that beg to be shared.

    What does it mean?

    A bunch is a first collective noun: many small things, one word. A child who says “bunch of grapes” is packaging dozens of objects into one idea — the same packing that later handles families, flocks and alphabet letters. The sharing game adds the social layer: counting out one-for-you is turn-taking with snacks.

    What does the child need to know?

    Three things to gather before the first grape: the word itself, said at the card; the climbing story, told with a hand that rises — vines go up and up, hanging their heavy bunches from wires — and one counted sharing round. Then the kitchen rule, said plainly and kindly: at your house, a grown-up cuts grapes small, every time, and everyone eats sitting down.

    Why this matters

    Grapes carry the set’s most important safety conversation, and the card is the kindest place to have it: the fruit is beloved, so the rule attaches to something warm. Cut-small-and-sit-down is a habit built by calm repetition, and this lesson starts it early, without a single scare.

    What it teaches

    Counting and one-to-one sharing, collective-noun awareness (a bunch), turn-taking, safe-eating habits rehearsed positively, and vine-and-climbing plant knowledge that diversifies the growing stories.

    Words to learn

    grapespurplebunchshareroundsweet

    Say this to your child

    ““Grapes! A whole bunch of them — one, two, three... too many to count! They grow on vines that climb and climb. Now the kitchen rule: we wash them, a grown-up cuts them small, and we sit down to share. One for you... one for me... what a polite little fruit!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say grapes — then ask how many grapes are on the card: more than you can count quickly? That is why the word is a bunch-word.
    2. Tell the growing story: grapes grow on vines that climb, hanging in heavy bunches — farms build them wire roads to travel.
    3. Washing job: your child rinses the bunch in the colander while you explain today’s kitchen rule — a grown-up cuts them small, every time.
    4. The sharing round: cut grapes in a small bowl, and count out one for you, one for me, taking turns until the bowl wins.
    5. End sitting down, finishing together — the rule and the game wear the same chair.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a bunch of purple grapes with the word grapes underneath. Ask your child how many grapes they can point to, whether the bunch is bigger at the top or the bottom, and what color the grapes are.

    Ask your child

    “What do we call many grapes together?” “Where do grapes grow — on vines or on the ground?” “Who cuts them small?” “Where do we sit to eat them?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might count out sharing portions for the whole family, dolls included, or police the cutting rule with delight — “wait, cut them small!” — a safety habit repeated by the child is the safest kind there is.

    Out in the real world

    Grapes appear weekly: the fruit bowl, the lunchbox, the picnic. Each bunch is another round of the sharing game and another quiet rehearsal of the kitchen rule — repetition dressed as generosity.

    Try it together

    The sharing bowl: a grown-up cuts the washed grapes small into a little dish, and you take turns picking one each — one for you, one for me — counting the rounds until the bowl runs dry. The counting is real, the turn-taking is the deeper game, and sitting down together is the rule that never moves.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What is a whole lot of grapes called? Where do they grow? Who cuts them, and where do we eat?” A bunch, vines, the grown-up, and sat down — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If cutting feels like fuss, reframe it as bunch service: the knife comes out so the sharing bowl can be refilled. The rule sticks best when it sounds like hospitality rather than homework, and your child will pass it on to visitors.

    Staying safe

    This is the card that carries the rule: whole grapes are a choking risk for small children, so a grown-up cuts them lengthwise into small pieces, every time, and everyone eats sitting down. The habit is calm, quick and permanent — and it belongs to this fruit specifically.

    This lesson pairs with the Grapes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Watermelon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Watermelon is the fruit that arrives like an event: enormous, heavy, and full of three colors that the other cards spent a whole class teaching. This lesson teaches the long word at the card, the growing — on the ground, on sprawling vines — and the tap-and-name game that turns a slice into a color review.

    What is this?

    A watermelon is a huge fruit that grows on the ground on trailing vines, resting on the soil until picked. The card shows a slice: green rind, red flesh, black seeds. The word is long — wa-ter-mel-on — and worth clapping out, because four parts is the longest rhythm in the fruit class.

    What does it mean?

    One slice, three colors: green, red, black — a watermelon is a color lesson wearing a snack. A child who names all three while tapping the slice is doing multi-property description — size, color, position — and the fruit makes the description feel like a drum solo instead of a test.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word clapped at the card, the ground-growing story — this fruit does not climb or hang, it lounges — and one tap-and-name round on a real slice: tap the green, tap the red, tap a seed. Then the tasting: a grown-up cuts, cold wedges are served, and summer officially begins.

    Why this matters

    Multi-word description is the bridge from naming to telling: “the red part”, “the green outside”, “the black seeds” are little sentences about one object. Watermelon is the friendliest place to practise, because the object is delicious and the parts are unmissable.

    What it teaches

    Multi-property description (color and position), syllable clapping on a four-part word, size vocabulary (enormous, heavy), summer-food culture, and patient waiting — the biggest fruit in the shop also has the longest queue to the table.

    Words to learn

    watermelonredgreenseedsbigsummer

    Say this to your child

    ““Watermelon! Wa-ter-mel-on — four claps for the biggest fruit we know! It grows on the ground, resting like a sunbather. Look at the slice: green outside, red inside, black seeds — three colors in one snack. Tap them and name them... now the best part: the crunching!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and clap the word out — wa-ter-mel-on, four claps, the longest word in the fruit class, said twice.
    2. Tell the growing story: watermelons grow on the ground on sprawling vines — no climbing, no hanging, just lounging in the sun until big.
    3. The tap-and-name game on the card: tap the green rind and say green, tap the red flesh and say red, tap a seed and say black.
    4. Real-slice round: a grown-up cuts a wedge, and your child taps and names all three colors before the first bite.
    5. Eat cold, and rate the seeds — count how many ride home on the slice. The word got clapped; the colors got named; summer got eaten.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card together: it shows a watermelon slice with green rind, red flesh and black seeds, with the word watermelon underneath. Ask your child to point at each color in turn, and where the black seeds are sitting.

    Ask your child

    “How many claps does the word need?” “Where does a watermelon grow — up a tree or on the ground?” “What are the three colors in one slice?” “Which color is the outside?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might clap out wa-ter-mel-on for days, tap-tap-tap every fruit in the bowl, or report that the watermelon is “sleeping on the ground” — a fruit described as a sunbather is a fruit whose biography has been understood.

    Out in the real world

    Watermelons headline the summer: picnics, barbecues, the shop where whole ones sit like boulders. Each meeting repeats the long word and the three-color game — the loudest vocabulary lesson of the warm months, served cold.

    Try it together

    The three-color drum: a grown-up cuts a cold wedge, and your child taps it like a drum — tap the green and say green, tap the red and say red, tap a seed and say black — before the first bite. Then the seed count: how many rode home on the slice? Count them off the plate, and eat the winnings.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Clap the long word. Where does it grow? Name the three colors in a slice.” Four claps, the ground, and green-red-black — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the four claps tangle, drop to two — mel-on — and grow the word back one clap at a time over the week. Long words are stairs, not walls, and every child climbs them at their own pace.

    Staying safe

    The cutting is all grown-up work: a whole watermelon defeats adult knives, so no small hands go near the job. Cold wedges for little eaters get served seeded or spooned, sitting down — the biggest fruit obeys the same sit-down rule as the smallest.

    This lesson pairs with the Watermelon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Pineapple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The pineapple is the fruit bowl’s royalty: a golden body under armor, wearing a green crown, hiding a secret — it grows in the ground, not in trees, crown or no crown. This lesson teaches the word at the card, the secret, and the touch test that makes the bumpy-skin comparison unforgettable.

    What is this?

    A pineapple is a big golden fruit with a tough, spiky, diamond-patterned skin and a crown of stiff green leaves. The card shows a yellow pineapple with its spiky green crown. It grows on a leafy plant close to the ground in warm countries — the crown is pure decoration.

    What does it mean?

    The pineapple’s secret — ground fruit, tree-looking crown — teaches children that appearances write wrong stories: what looks like a tree-fruit is a ground-fruit. A child who enjoys being told a plant secret is learning that the natural world has hidden facts, and that knowing them is a pleasure, not a chore.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the secret — in the ground, on a plant, despite the crown — and the touch test: bumpy, hard pineapple, then smooth, soft banana. Two fruits, two skins, one lesson in describing surfaces. The tasting waits for a grown-up, because nobody peels armor with little hands.

    Why this matters

    Contrast descriptions — bumpy versus smooth, hard versus soft — are early science language, and the fruit bowl supplies the pairs. A child who can say “the pineapple is bumpy and the banana is smooth” has built a comparison sentence, which is grammar and observation holding hands.

    What it teaches

    Tactile vocabulary (bumpy, spiky, hard, smooth), contrast descriptions in full sentences, botanical myth-busting (ground fruit, not tree fruit), patience while the grown-up does the armor-peeling, and tropical-plant curiosity.

    Words to learn

    pineapplecrownspikygoldensweetbumpy

    Say this to your child

    ““Pineapple! Look at it — it wears a CROWN! But here is the secret: it grows down in the soil, not up in a tree. Feel the skin — bumpy! Hard! Like armor. And inside, it is golden and sweet. The grown-up opens the armor; we do the tasting and the crowning.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say pineapple — then ask what the fruit is wearing on its head. A crown! Say the word again like a royal announcement.
    2. Tell the secret: despite the crown, pineapples grow in the ground on leafy plants in warm countries. Say it like gossip — children keep plant secrets well.
    3. The touch test, hands washed: feel a real pineapple — bumpy, hard, heavy — then a banana — smooth, soft, light. Say both pairs out loud.
    4. The tasting is a grown-up job from end to end: the skin comes off with a big knife, and your child receives golden rounds or chunks, washed hands, sitting down.
    5. Close with the crown: draw or cut a paper crown for the fruit bowl’s new monarch — the word got said, the secret got kept, the throne got decorated.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a yellow pineapple with a spiky green crown and the word pineapple underneath. Ask your child to find the crown, count the spiky leaves they can see, and say what the skin’s pattern reminds them of.

    Ask your child

    “Does a pineapple grow in trees or in the ground?” “What is the fruit wearing on its head?” “Which is bumpy — the pineapple or the banana?” “Who gets to do the cutting?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might retell the ground-secret to anyone who visits, stroke the bumpy skin like a museum piece, or appoint the fruit bowl’s pineapple “the king” — a fruit with a title and a biography is a fruit whose word has moved in permanently.

    Out in the real world

    Pineapples appear whole in the shop and pre-cut in tubs, and either way the word rehearses: crown up, crown off, armor and all. The bumpy-versus-smooth game extends to the whole kitchen — oranges, coconuts in books, the family dog.

    Try it together

    The touch museum: a whole pineapple, crown and all, travels from hand to hand — bumpy! hard! heavy! — next to a smooth banana for contrast, while your child announces each feeling like a tour guide. The grown-up removes the armor later; the tasting is golden chunks, eaten sitting down like royalty.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Where does a pineapple grow — the secret? What does it wear? Who peels the armor?” The ground, the crown and “the grown-up” — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child refuses the first chunk — pineapples tingle — say why: the fruit carries a tiny bite of its own, a little acid that tickles. Naming the tingle turns a refusal into a sensation worth investigating, and the second chunk often goes down as research.

    Staying safe

    Pineapple armor is strictly a grown-up job: the skin is tough, the knife is big, and the crown is spikier than it looks. Small eaters receive peeled, cored chunks — and the crown itself stays decorative, not chewable.

    This lesson pairs with the Pineapple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Mango — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The mango is the fruit class’s dessert course: golden, soft when ready, and pronounced with the mmmmm already built in. Two rituals make the fruit unforgettable — the gentle cheek-squeeze that judges ripeness, and the treasure hunt for the big flat seed — while the biography goes up: mangoes ripen on trees in hot countries, in real sunshine.

    What is this?

    A mango is a golden-yellow fruit, blushing orange-red where the sun caught it, that grows on trees in hot countries. The card shows a yellow-orange mango with a green leaf. Inside is soft, sweet flesh — and one big, flat seed in the middle, like a treasure the fruit was guarding.

    What does it mean?

    Ripeness is a first physics of food: firm means wait, soft-gently means ready. A child who squeezes a mango like a cheek and reports “not yet” or “ready!” is reading fruit by feel — the same judging that later picks pears and avocados, started young on the sweetest possible subject.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word said slowly and hungrily at the card, the tree story — mangoes grow up in the sunshine in hot countries — and the squeeze ritual: one gentle press, like testing a cheek. The seed hunt lands at tasting: a grown-up washes, cuts around the stone, and your child discovers the treasure in the middle.

    Why this matters

    Words with built-in sound play — mmmmm-mango — get rehearsed for the pleasure of the sound alone, and pleasure-rehearsed words stick. Add the ripeness judging and the seed discovery, and one fruit has supplied sound play, sensory science and a treasure story. Few cards earn their keep this thoroughly.

    What it teaches

    Sensory judging (firm versus soft), gentle-touch control, tropical tree knowledge, sound-play pronunciation, and the narrative pleasure of a fruit with a hidden treasure that explains why the cutting is a grown-up job.

    Words to learn

    mangogoldensoftsweetseedtropical

    Say this to your child

    ““Mmmmm-mango! Say it slowly — it is the sweetest word in the fruit bowl. Mangoes grow on trees in the hot sunshine. Is ours ready? Squeeze it gently, like a cheek... soft! Ready! Now a grown-up will cut it, and we will find the treasure — one big flat seed, hidden in the middle!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say mango the slow way — mmmmm-mango — letting the hunger show in your voice. Repeat until your child joins the slow club.
    2. Tell the growing story: mangoes grow on trees in hot countries, ripening in real sunshine until golden.
    3. The squeeze test: your child presses one finger gently against a real mango, like testing a cheek — firm means wait, softly-giving means ready. Report the verdict.
    4. The tasting is staged: a grown-up washes the fruit and cuts around the middle, and your child hunts the treasure — one big, flat seed, discovered and admired.
    5. Close with the golden round-up: what else at snack time is golden? The pineapple card will agree.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a yellow-orange mango with a green leaf and the word mango underneath. Ask your child which colors they can see on the skin, where the leaf sits, and what shape the fruit makes.

    Ask your child

    “How do we say the sweetest word — fast or slow?” “Where do mangoes grow?” “How do we test if one is ready?” “What hides in the middle?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might pronounce mmmmm-mango at every meal for a week, squeeze-test everything soft in the bowl, or present the discovered seed like a trophy — the treasure story does heavy lifting, and children retell it with the pride of real explorers.

    Out in the real world

    Mangos appear seasonally: whole in the shop, cubed in tubs, dried in packets. Every meeting rehearses the slow word and the squeeze test — and any seed found at home is a treasure twice, the second time for free.

    Try it together

    The ripeness panel: two mangos, one gentle squeeze each — your child presses like testing a cheek and delivers the verdict: not yet, or ready! The chosen one gets cut around the stone by a grown-up, and the big flat seed becomes a trophy to hold and admire before the golden cubes disappear.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Say the sweetest word slowly. Where do mangoes grow? What hides in the middle?” The mmmm, the trees and the big flat seed — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If no fresh mango is available, the dried version carries the lesson: same word, same sweetness, tougher chew. The squeeze test can wait for the next fresh one — vocabulary does not keep a calendar.

    Staying safe

    The cutting is grown-up work from wash to plate: mangoes have a big, hard, slippery stone in the middle, and the knife work around it takes practice even for adults. Little eaters get soft cubes, washed hands, and the seed handed over after the danger has left the room.

    This lesson pairs with the Mango flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Carrot — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The carrot opens the vegetable half of the class with its best trick: it grows hiding underground, pointy end down, leafy hair up. This lesson teaches the word at the card, the below-the-soil story, and the top-and-tail observation that makes the vegetable’s shape a small mystery solved.

    What is this?

    A carrot is a long, pointy, orange root vegetable that grows underground, with feathery green leaves showing above the soil. The card shows an orange carrot with a leafy green top. Rabbits agree it is excellent. The orange inside it is the same sunshine-colored stuff that makes it good for eyes.

    What does it mean?

    Root vegetables introduce the idea that food has a hidden half: what you see above ground is only the address, and the meal waits below. A child who understands that carrots grow down and beans grow up has a first map of the vegetable world — and maps make new vegetables easier to meet.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the underground story — the orange part hides in the dark soil, the leafy top catches sun — and one full crunchy tasting: washed, topped, tailed and cut into sticks by a grown-up, then crunched like a rabbit. The loud crunch is the vegetable class’s signature sound.

    Why this matters

    The carrot’s shape invites description work: pointy at the bottom, leafy at the top, long all over. Describing parts and directions — top, bottom, pointy, leafy — builds the spatial vocabulary that later handles “put the book on the bottom shelf” without a demonstration.

    What it teaches

    Spatial and part vocabulary (top, bottom, pointy, leafy), underground-versus-above-ground plant knowledge, loud confident chewing, washing routine ownership, and the rabbit-connection that makes vegetables storybook material.

    Words to learn

    carrotorangeundergroundrootcrunchtop

    Say this to your child

    ““Carrot! Long and orange and pointy — and it grows HIDING underground! The green hair sticks up, the orange part points down into the dark. Rabbits pull them up. Now we wash it, a grown-up cuts it into sticks... CRUNCH! Can you crunch like a rabbit? Louder! The rabbits will hear!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say carrot — then ask which end was underground: the orange point or the leafy top? Let your child guess before you tell.
    2. Tell the growing story: the orange part grows down in the dark soil, hiding; the leafy top grows up in the sun. Pull-the-carrot is the classic farm picture for a reason.
    3. Top-and-tail observation: hold a real carrot and find both ends — the pointy bottom that lived underground, the cut top where the leaves were.
    4. Tasting job: your child washes the carrots while a grown-up tops, tails and cuts sticks — then everyone crunches like rabbits, loudly.
    5. Close with the orange round-up: what else is orange? The orange fruit card matches — one word, two foods, both orange on purpose.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows an orange carrot with a green leafy top and the word carrot underneath. Ask your child which end is wider, what the top looks like, and what color the whole vegetable is.

    Ask your child

    “Where does the orange part grow — up or down?” “What shows above the soil?” “Who else loves carrots?” “What do we do before we crunch?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might pull pretend carrots from the sofa cushions, crunch sticks with theatrical rabbit noises, or inspect the leafy tops at the shop — a vegetable with a direction story gets retold pointing down, every time.

    Out in the real world

    Carrots repeat all year: sticks in lunchboxes, rounds in stews, the whole ones with feather tops at the market. Each meeting rehearses the word, the direction story and the crunch — the most reliable vegetable in the drawer.

    Try it together

    The rabbit crunch contest: washed carrot sticks cut by a grown-up, and everyone crunched like rabbits — loudest and longest crunch wins the crown. Then cooked rounds get a turn: soft and quiet, same word. Loud versus soft, raw versus cooked — the carrot teaches both and the rabbits eat the evidence.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Where does a carrot grow? What shows above the ground? Show me a rabbit crunch.” Down in the dark, the leafy top, and a loud demonstration — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child avoids raw sticks but accepts cooked rounds, serve both and describe the difference: cooked is soft, raw is loud. Both are the same word, and either one keeps the lesson alive at dinner.

    Staying safe

    Carrots for small eaters are washed, topped and cut by a grown-up — sticks for confident chewers, thinner batons for the newest ones, and grated for the very smallest. Whole raw carrots are a chewing challenge, so the cutting board belongs to the adults.

    This lesson pairs with the Carrot flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Potato — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The potato is the vegetable children have eaten most and noticed least: chips, mash, jackets — all potatoes, all disguised. Underground is the address this lesson hands over — the same dark hiding place the carrot chose — and the great transformation is the main event: one dusty, hard, raw potato becomes every soft, steaming dinner food.

    What is this?

    A potato is a round-ish, brown, spotty vegetable that grows underground on plants whose leaves show above the soil. The card shows a spotty brown one with its word beneath. Raw, it is hard and dusty; cooked, it is soft and steaming — and the spots, given time and soil, could grow into whole new plants.

    What does it mean?

    The raw-to-cooked transformation is kitchen physics at its most visible: same potato, two completely different feelings. A child who holds a raw potato and then eats mash has watched matter change state with their own hands — the beginning of cooking literacy, and of why-humans-cook conversations.

    What does the child need to know?

    Two facts carry this lesson: the potato grows in the dark below the soil, the same hiding habit as the carrot, and it exists in two states — hard and dusty raw, soft and steaming cooked — so both get met, one held and one tasted. Then the delight: the little spots are called eyes, and yes, that is exactly as wonderful as it sounds.

    Why this matters

    Potato connects the card to nearly every dinner your child has ever eaten, which makes it a vocabulary multiplier: mash, chips, jackets and roasties are all this word in costumes. Naming the root food behind the disguises gives a child power over the whole menu.

    What it teaches

    State-change observation (raw versus cooked), tactile comparison (hard and dusty versus soft and steaming), underground-growing knowledge shared with the carrot, part vocabulary (spots, eyes, skin), and menu-connected word power.

    Words to learn

    potatobrownspotsundergroundhardsoft

    Say this to your child

    ““Potato! Po-TAY-to! Brown and spotty and hiding underground — just like the carrot. Feel this raw one: hard! Dusty! Now taste dinner: soft, warm mash — same potato! It changed in the cooking. And the little spots? Those are its EYES. A potato with eyes — imagine!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say potato with a bounce — po-TAY-to — then ask where it grows and wait: underground, like the carrot, hiding in the dark.
    2. The eyes hunt: find the little spots on the card and on a real potato — those spots are called eyes, and planted in soil each one could become a whole new plant.
    3. The raw hold: pass the raw potato around — heavy, hard, dusty — and let everyone describe it in one word each.
    4. The cooked reveal: serve the softest thing on the menu — mash, a jacket, soft boiled rounds — and compare: same potato, completely different feeling. Say both words: hard, soft.
    5. Close with the count: how many potato dinners can your child name from this week? Mash counts. Chips count. The word has been busy.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card together: it shows a brown, spotty potato with the word potato underneath. Ask your child to count the spots they can see, what shape the potato is closest to, and whether the skin looks smooth or rough.

    Ask your child

    “Where does a potato grow?” “What are the little spots called?” “Which is hard — raw or cooked?” “What potato dinners did we eat this week?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might hunt for eyes on every potato in the bag, demand “the hard one” to hold at dinner, or announce that chips are potatoes wearing costumes — a menu decoded is a vocabulary lesson winning.

    Out in the real world

    Potatoes dominate the week invisibly: mash on Monday, chips on Friday, the jackets at the weekend. Naming them all as the same word gives your child the biggest harvest in the vegetable drawer — one word, dozens of dinners.

    Try it together

    The potato double-act: hold the raw one — hard, dusty, heavy — and pass it around with one describing word each, then eat the softest possible mash from the same bag. Hard then soft, raw then cooked: your child just watched a transformation and named both of its endings at one meal.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Where do potatoes grow? What are the spots called? Which is soft — raw or cooked?” Underground, eyes, and the cooked one — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child only recognises chips as potato, line the evidence up gently: mash, a boiled round, a raw one. Same word all the way down the table — and the moment the penny drops, dinner becomes a revision lesson forever.

    Staying safe

    Raw potatoes are for holding, not chewing — the cooking does the digestible work, so the tasting is always the cooked version. The washing, peeling and boiling are grown-up jobs, and small hands get the describe-and-compare roles instead.

    This lesson pairs with the Potato flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Tomato — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The tomato is the shiniest card in the vegetable half and the owner of the class’s best argument: scientists call it a fruit because it grows from a flower, cooks call it a vegetable because it lives in dinner. This lesson teaches the word, the vine it grows on, and the little green crown every tomato wears.

    What is this?

    A tomato is a round, red, shiny fruit-vegetable that grows on vines in gardens and greenhouses, wearing a small green star where the stem held it. The card shows a round red tomato with a green stem. In this class it sits with the vegetables, where the kitchen has always kept it.

    What does it mean?

    The tomato’s double identity is a child’s first famous argument, and it teaches the useful idea that names can depend on who is talking: scientists vote fruit, cooks vote vegetable, and both are allowed. A child who enjoys the argument has met the idea that knowledge has committees — and that they can join the debate.

    What does the child need to know?

    For this card, gather three things: the word, the garden picture — tomato plants lean on sticks, climbing and hanging their fruit — and the crown hunt, because every tomato, card or real, wears a little green crown on top. The tasting completes it: washed, crowns off, sliced by a grown-up, and admired shiny side up before the first bite.

    Why this matters

    The shiny skin makes tomatoes the best light-study in the bowl: where does the shine come from? A small mirror conversation at snack time — light bouncing off the smooth skin — is early physics delivered on a food your child will eat anyway.

    What it teaches

    Observation of light and shine, vine-and-stick plant knowledge, the two-committee idea (fruit or vegetable, depending on the speaker), gentle handling of round rolling things, and the confidence to hold a small opinion in an adult argument.

    Words to learn

    tomatoredroundvineshinycrown

    Say this to your child

    ““Tomato! Say it twice — tomato, tomahto — both are right! It grows on a vine in the garden, hanging shiny and red. Look, every tomato wears a little green crown, right on top. Find the crown! Now wash it, a grown-up slices it... look how it SHINES. Round, red, and dressed for dinner.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say tomato twice, two ways — tomato, tomahto — and announce that both are correct, which children find scandalous and delightful.
    2. Tell the growing story: tomatoes grow on vines in gardens, hanging like little lanterns, with sticks to lean on when they get heavy.
    3. The crown hunt: find the little green star on the card’s tomato, then on every real tomato in the house — every single one wears one.
    4. The roll test, gently: round things roll. One slow roll across the table, caught before the edge — shiny, round and in a hurry.
    5. The tasting: your child washes the tomatoes while a grown-up takes the crowns off and slices them. Admire the shine first, then eat it.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card together: it shows a round red tomato with a green stem and the word tomato underneath. Ask your child where the green part sits, what the shine on the skin could be, and what shape the tomato is.

    Ask your child

    “What does every tomato wear on top?” “Where do tomatoes grow — on vines or underground?” “Is it a fruit or a vegetable — what does the kitchen say?” “What happens if we roll it?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might hunt crowns on every tomato for a week, referee the fruit-versus-vegetable argument at dinner, or roll one around the plate announcing — “a tomato!” — with a straight face. The argument is the lesson’s encore, and children love being its judge.

    Out in the real world

    Tomatoes live in everything: salads, sauces, the pasta tonight, the ketchup tomorrow. Naming the round red original behind the sauces gives your child the source code of half the dinner table — one word, many disguises, all delicious.

    Try it together

    The crown hunt: three tomatoes on the table, and your child inspects each one for its little green crown, then rolls them — very gently — across the table to prove that round things roll. A grown-up crowns and slices for tasting, and the shiny red rounds get admired before the first juicy bite.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What does a tomato wear on top? Where does it grow? What do scientists and cooks disagree about?” The crown, the vine, and the famous argument — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child picks tomato pieces out of everything, keep the word alive anyway: name it in sauces, soups and ketchup. Recognition does not require eating — and the sauce-tomato connection is a genuine decoding skill the kitchen hands out free.

    Staying safe

    The crowns come off with a grown-up’s hands and the slicing too — small round things and knives are an adult meeting. Cherry tomatoes for the smallest eaters get quartered lengthwise, and the shine is for admiring before the chewing begins.

    This lesson pairs with the Tomato flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Cucumber — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The cucumber is the vegetable class’s quiet science kit: cool to the touch, mostly water inside, and wearing the same bumpy green skin as its famous cousin the watermelon. This lesson teaches the word at the card, the trailing-vine growing, and the cool-slice trick that turns snack time into a temperature experiment.

    What is this?

    A cucumber is a long, green, cylinder-shaped vegetable that grows on trailing vines along the ground or up supports. The card shows a long green cucumber. It is cool to the touch and crunchy inside because it is mostly water — which is exactly why it feels like the fridge’s favorite vegetable.

    What does it mean?

    Cucumber teaches hidden water: a crunchy vegetable that is secretly a drink. A child who learns that cucumbers are mostly water has planted the idea that foods have insides with jobs — water for cooling, sunshine-colors for eyes, in the carrot’s case — and food science starts exactly there.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the vine story — cucumbers trail along the ground like the watermelon, their cousin — and the cool trick: hold a slice against the back of a hand and report the temperature. Then the tasting: washed, cut by a grown-up into coins or sticks, crunched cool.

    Why this matters

    The cousin comparison — cucumber and watermelon, same bumpy green skin — is early classification: families exist in the vegetable drawer. A child who spots the skin similarity has done real botany with their eyes, and the reward is knowing a secret about two foods at once.

    What it teaches

    Temperature awareness (cool, cold, room-warm), hidden-water science, plant-family classification by skin, crunchy chewing, and the descriptive vocabulary of long, smooth, green and striped.

    Words to learn

    cucumbergreenlongcoolcrunchywater

    Say this to your child

    ““Cucumber! Cue-cum-ber — the chilliest vegetable in the bowl! It grows on a vine, trailing along the ground like its cousin the watermelon. Look at the skins — same bumpy green! Now feel this slice on your hand... cool! That is the water inside, having a rest. Crunch, crunch, cold, cold!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say cucumber in three beats — cue-cum-ber — a cool word for a cool vegetable, said with a shivery voice.
    2. Tell the growing story: cucumbers grow on vines that trail along the ground — the same plan as their big cousin, the watermelon.
    3. The skin comparison: look at the card, then at the watermelon card — same bumpy green skin, one long and one round. Families look alike.
    4. The cool trick: a grown-up cuts one slice, and your child holds it against the back of their hand — cool! Cucumbers are mostly water; that is the fridge feeling.
    5. Tasting: coins or sticks, crunched cold, and the verdict collected — is the inside as cool as the outside? Science says yes.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a long green cucumber with the word cucumber underneath. Ask your child whether the cucumber is straight or curved, what the skin’s color does from end to end, and how long it looks next to the other cards.

    Ask your child

    “Why does a cucumber feel cool?” “Who is the cucumber’s big cousin?” “Where do cucumbers grow — on vines or in trees?” “What does the inside mostly hold — water or sand?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might hold cucumber slices to various warm body parts as emergency cooling, report the watermelon kinship to anyone nearby, or crunch coins with a shiver-noise — a temperature fact discovered by hand is a temperature fact kept for life.

    Out in the real world

    Cucumbers repeat all summer: salads, sticks in lunchboxes, the raita side at dinner. Every slice is another cool trick and another cousin citation — the most refreshing repetition in the vegetable drawer.

    Try it together

    The coolness experiment: a grown-up cuts two coins of cucumber, your child lays one on the back of each hand, and the verdict comes in — cool! colder than the room! Then the taste test: crunchy, wet, quiet. Mostly-water science, with a snack for a conclusion that usually gets eaten.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Why is a cucumber cool? Who is its cousin? Where does it grow?” The water inside, the watermelon, and the trailing vine — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child rejects the crunch, serve the coins peeled — the skin’s bumpy texture is a common dealbreaker, and the cool-water crunch underneath converts more skeptics than argument ever will.

    Staying safe

    Slices and sticks are a grown-up’s cutting work, and the ends get trimmed off before serving — the stem end can taste bitter, and life is short. Whole cucumbers are for holding and comparing, not for biting like apples at this age.

    This lesson pairs with the Cucumber flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Broccoli — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Broccoli is the vegetable class’s imagination magnet: hold it upside down and it is a tree, point it at the sky and it is a forest, eat a branch and it is dinner. This lesson teaches the word at the card, the real secret — those lumpy bits are hundreds of flower buds — and the tree game that makes the tasting an adventure.

    What is this?

    Broccoli is a green vegetable with a thick stalk and a lumpy, bushy top made of hundreds of tiny buds — it grows above the ground in cool gardens, standing up like a small shrub. The card shows a green broccoli that looks like a little tree. It is a flower your child is allowed to eat.

    What does it mean?

    The tree pretence is not a detour from learning — it is the learning: a child who plays at being a giant eating a forest is doing symbolic play, the engine of language. The word broccoli rides on every branch, every chomp and every roar, and pretend-loaded words get more rehearsals than plain ones.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the flower secret — the lumpy top is hundreds of tiny buds, which is why it feels like a forest floor — and the upside-down game: hold it by the stalk, trunk to the sky, and take bites off the branches. Then the tasting: washed by your child, cut by a grown-up, trees for dinner.

    Why this matters

    Pretend play is the cheapest motivator in the parenting toolkit, and broccoli supplies the prop for free: tree, forest, tiny clouds, a green microphone. A child who eats a tree for dinner is eating a vegetable they refused last week — the costume changed, and so did the vote.

    What it teaches

    Symbolic and pretend play, botanical secret knowledge (flower buds), part vocabulary (stalk, branches, buds), confident chewing of a challenging texture, and the storytelling that turns dinner into a nature documentary.

    Words to learn

    broccoligreentreeflowerbudscrunch

    Say this to your child

    ““Broccoli! A little tree — and you can EAT it! Look at the bumpy top: those are hundreds of tiny flower buds, all packed together. Hold it upside down — trunk at the top! Now be a giant: chomp a branch, chomp a branch... the forest never stood a chance. Trees have never been this delicious.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say broccoli — then ask what it looks like. A tree! Agree enthusiastically; the resemblance is the lesson’s engine.
    2. Tell the secret: the lumpy top is made of hundreds of tiny flower buds — broccoli is a flower your child is allowed to eat, and the bumpy bits are the proof.
    3. The tree game: hold a real floret upside down by the stalk — trunk up, branches down — and be a giant taking bites off the forest. Roar between bites.
    4. The washing job: your child rinses the florets in the colander, leaf-forest to tap, while a grown-up stands by for the cutting.
    5. Tasting: cut florets, raw crunch first, then the soft steamed version — same tree, two weathers. Which forest does the giant prefer?

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card together: it shows a green broccoli with a lumpy top and the word broccoli underneath. Ask your child what the top looks like, whether the card’s broccoli has a trunk at the bottom, and what color the whole vegetable is.

    Ask your child

    “What does broccoli look like?” “What are the lumpy bits really — leaves, buds or stones?” “Where does it grow — up in the air or under the ground?” “Which is your giant roar — loud or louder?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might demand “tree pieces” by name at dinner, stage forests on the plate with mashed-potato ground, or take enormous giant-bites with sound effects — the pretence is the point, and the vegetable is the beneficiary.

    Out in the real world

    Broccoli repeats weekly: florets in pasta, trees on the dinner plate, the tiny ones in stir-fries. Each appearance is another chance to play giant — and a vegetable that comes with a game built in gets eaten on a different schedule than one that does not.

    Try it together

    The broccoli forest: hold it upside down — trunk to the sky — and walk a finger along the branches, naming the florets like trees, then take one bite per branch until the forest shrinks. Washed by your child first, cut by a grown-up after: a tree you are allowed to eat is a tree worth meeting twice.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What does broccoli look like? What are the bumpy bits? Who is brave enough to be the giant?” A tree, flower buds, and a volunteering mouth — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the tree game converts a refuser, retire it slowly rather than banning it: from giant-bites to forest-bites to just-broccoli, over weeks. The pretence is scaffolding, and scaffolding comes down a piece at a time when the wall stands.

    Staying safe

    The stalk skin is tough, so a grown-up peels and cuts the florets into tree-sized pieces — raw for confident crunchers, steamed for the rest. The washing is your child’s proud job; the knife work stays firmly in the grown-up camp.

    This lesson pairs with the Broccoli flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Fruits & Vegetables Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FRUITS & VEGETABLES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Corn — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Corn is the vegetable class’s puzzle box: a cob of golden kernels wearing a green husk like wrapping paper. This lesson teaches the word at the card, the tall-stalk growing story, and the unwrap-and-munch routine — peel the leaves, count the rows, munch across a line like a tiny typewriter.

    What is this?

    Corn is a tall grass that grows in fields on thick stalks, higher than a child’s head, wearing long green leaves. The card shows a yellow corn cob with green husk leaves. Every yellow kernel is a seed; the kernels sit in straight rows; and the husk is the packaging the plant grew itself.

    What does it mean?

    Corn is pattern made edible: rows, lines, symmetry — a natural grid a child can hold. A child who munches “across a row” is reading a structure left to right, the exact motion reading will ask for later, practised here on a cob with butter. The rows are a gift; use them.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the card, the tall-stalk story — corn grows higher than your head in fields, one cob per stalk — and the unwrap ritual: peel the husk leaves back like a present, then find the rows. The tasting is a grown-up-cooked cob, cooled, and munched across the rows.

    Why this matters

    Unwrapping the husk is delayed gratification with a payoff: the present is food, the paper is a plant. Children who work to open their food value it differently — and the husk-to-kernel reveal teaches, without one word of lecture, that food comes packaged by nobody but nature.

    What it teaches

    Pattern reading on a real object (rows and lines), unwrap sequencing, munch-across-the-row fine motor, tall-plant field knowledge, and the patience that unwrapping a present — a plant-grown present — quietly builds.

    Words to learn

    cornyellowkernelshuskrowscob

    Say this to your child

    ““Corn! A cob of little yellow bricks, all in a row. It grows on tall, tall stalks — higher than your head! — and hides in green wrapping paper. Unwrap it: leaf by leaf. Now the rows — count one, then MUNCH across a line, left to right, like a typewriter. Typewriter munching is the only correct way!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say corn — then ask how many yellow kernels your child can count before losing track. Too many! That is why they come in rows.
    2. Tell the growing story: corn grows on tall stalks in fields — higher than your head — with long leaves, and the cobs hide inside them.
    3. The unwrap: your child peels the husk leaves back, one by one, like unwrapping a present — the plant wrapped it itself. Announce each leaf.
    4. The row hunt: find the straight lines of kernels — count a row across the top, then run a finger down one full line like a ladder.
    5. The tasting: a grown-up cooks the cob and cools it, and your child munches across one row, left to right, like a tiny typewriter. Ding!

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: it shows a yellow corn cob with green husk leaves and the word corn underneath. Ask your child whether the husk is open or closed, how many kernels they can point to, and what the green leaves are doing on the card.

    Ask your child

    “What wraps the corn up?” “Where does corn grow — on bushes or on tall stalks?” “What is one yellow kernel if we plant it?” “Which way do we munch a row?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might unwrap any leaf-wrapped thing looking for kernels, munch typewriter rows with sound effects, or report that corn grows “taller than Daddy” — field-height is the fact that sticks, and it is accurate.

    Out in the real world

    Corn repeats all summer: cobs at barbecues, sweetcorn at picnics, the popcorn bag at the cinema. Every form is the same word in a different costume, and the row-munching trick upgrades every single cob for the rest of the season.

    Try it together

    The typewriter munch: a grown-up cooks and cools the cob, your child grips the ends and munches across one row of kernels — ding! — like a tiny typewriter, row by row. Between rows, count the empty lines. Nobody has ever finished this game without a very buttery grin.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What wraps a corn cob? Where does corn grow? Show me a typewriter munch.” The husk, the tall stalks, and a left-to-right demonstration — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the typewriter game stalls, invert it: your child drives the row, and you are the carriage that clacks at each kernel. The sillier the sound effects, the further down the row the munching goes — an engineered vegetable victory.

    Staying safe
